h1: The 8 Best Electric Spin Scrubbers for Tile and Grout of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Tile Grout Scrubbers 2026: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: eight cordless electric spin scrubbers for tile and grout, from a 1500RPM Qimedo to budget long-handle units, with head advice.
mainKeyword: electric spin scrubbers for tile and grout
summary: The Qimedo Q2 is our top pick for baked-on grout because it lists 1500RPM and a 4000mAh battery. The HOTO Wand is the one designed around grout lines, and the Leebein floor tile model is best for large floors. Budget shoppers can start with the Dovety.
intro: Grout is porous, and a soft brush skates over the dirt sitting inside it. The usual mistake is buying a scrubber for its motor and ignoring the brush head, when it is the bristle shape and stiffness that actually reach into a grout line.

We ranked eight cordless spin scrubbers from the listings, weighing motor speed and battery where they are given, then brush head count, handle reach, and angle adjustment. None of these claims comes from running them ourselves. Price range matters here, because a cheap scrubber with the right heads often beats a pricey one with the wrong ones.

products.name: Qimedo Electric Spin Scrubber Q2, 4000mAh Battery, 1500RPM High Power
products.verdict: The only scrubber here that publishes both speed and battery numbers.
products.description:
The Q2 lists a 1500RPM high-power motor and a 4000mAh battery, the strongest stated figures in this group. It falls in the $50 to $100 range.

It ranks first because stubborn, baked-on grout is the hard job, and a stated speed and battery size give you something concrete to rely on. Every rival below either hides those numbers or leans on accessories. The tradeoff is price, as this is the most expensive pick.

Choose it for dirty grout that has not been cleaned in years. The caveat is that more RPM means nothing without the right brush head, so pair it with a stiff grout brush.
products.idealFor: Heavy, baked-on grout and soap scum.

products.name: HOTO Wand Cordless Spin Scrubber, Electric Grout Brush, 12 Brush Heads
products.verdict: Named for grout work and packed with twelve brush heads.
products.description:
The HOTO Wand is called an electric grout brush, ships with 12 brush heads and runs cordless. It falls in the $25 to $50 range.

It ranks second because it is the only tool here framed around grout detail work, and twelve heads cover a lot of cases. It sits behind the Qimedo only because it gives no motor or battery figures.

Buy it if detail matters more than raw power. The caveat is that 12 heads is a lot to store and sort.
products.skipIf: You want published motor and battery numbers.

products.name: Leebein Electric Spin Scrubber, Cordless Powerful Scrub Brush for Cleaning Bathroom, Kitchen, Shower Tub and Floor Tile
products.verdict: Explicitly named for floor tile, with an adjustable extension handle.
products.description:
This Leebein is cordless, explicitly named for floor tile among other surfaces, and has an adjustable extension handle plus eight replaceable brush heads. It falls in the $25 to $50 range.

It ranks third because the extension handle saves your back on floors, which is where most tile lives. Against the HOTO, you trade a grout-first design for reach.

Choose it for kitchen and bathroom floors. The caveat is that eight heads and no listed motor figures leave power unclear.
products.skipIf: You mostly clean narrow grout lines.

products.name: Leebein Electric Spin Scrubber, Shower Scrubber with 4 Adjustable Angles and 8 Brush Heads, Remote Controller
products.verdict: Four angles and a remote make grout lines easier to attack.
products.description:
A scrubber with four adjustable head angles, eight brush heads and a remote controller. It falls in the $25 to $50 range.

It ranks fourth because the adjustable angle lets you approach grout from different directions, which is helpful in corners. It trails the other Leebein because the listing is built around showers, not floor tile.

Pick it for corners and wall tile. The caveat is that a remote is another small part to lose.
products.idealFor: Corners and wall tile with awkward angles.

products.name: TUYU Electric Spin Scrubber, 8 Replaceable Brush Heads for Home
products.verdict: A simple cordless set with eight swappable heads.
products.description:
The TUYU is a cordless scrubber for the home with eight replaceable brush heads. It falls in the $25 to $50 range.

It ranks fifth because it has fewer distinguishing features than the picks above, no angle control, no extension and no stated motor. What it offers is a plain way to switch between tile and grout heads.

Choose it for a basic all-purpose tool. The caveat is that nothing here sets it apart from cheaper options.
products.skipIf: You want angle control or reach.

products.name: Powerful Electric Spin Scrubber, Shower Scrubber with Long Handle
products.verdict: A long-handled scrubber that touts its motor.
products.description:
A shower scrubber with a powerful motor and a long handle that reduces manual scrubbing. It falls in the $25 to $50 range.

It ranks sixth because the motor is named but no speed is given, so the claim is hard to compare. The long handle spares your knees on low grout.

Buy it for stubborn buildup without bending. The caveat is the missing numbers and unclear brush head count.
products.skipIf: You want published speed or battery figures.

products.name: Dovety Electric Spin Scrubber, Extendable Handle, 8 Brush Heads
products.verdict: Eight heads and an extendable handle for under $25.
products.description:
The Dovety has an extendable handle and eight brush heads, and sits under $25, the lowest price here.

It ranks seventh because motor and battery details are missing, but the low price and generous head set make it a cheap way to find out whether you like spin scrubbing.

Choose it for light grout cleaning on a tight budget. The caveat is limited detail on power.

products.name: Electric Spin Scrubber for Bathroom, Shower Scrubber with Long Handle
products.verdict: A bare-bones bathroom scrubber with a long handle.
products.description:
A standalone electric scrubber with a long handle, built for bathrooms and priced under $25.

It ranks last because the listing offers the least detail on heads, motor or battery, so there is little to judge against the other picks. The long handle is its useful feature.

Pick it only for the lowest cost. The caveat is that you buy it largely unseen.
products.idealFor: A throwaway scrubber for a bathroom.
products.skipIf: You want to compare real specs.

whatMatters.detail: A grout line needs a stiff, narrow brush, while open tile can use a wide soft one. The wrong head wastes the motor. Look for the heads described in the bullets.
RPM is how fast the head spins. Higher speeds lift stuck grime, but control matters too. Check the listing for an RPM number.
Battery capacity in mAh sets runtime. A bigger number lasts through a whole bathroom. Look for the mAh figure.
Extension handles let you stand while scrubbing floors. Short handles are better for tight spots. Look for extendable or long handle wording.
Angle adjustment tilts the head to hit corners and edges. It saves awkward wrist positions. Look for a stated angle count.

faq.q: Does a spin scrubber really clean grout?
faq.a: It helps, especially with a stiff grout brush. Severe staining may still need a cleaner.

faq.q: What is the biggest buying mistake?
faq.a: Choosing on motor alone. The brush head decides how well it works in a grout line.
Not for light cleaning, but it helps with baked-on grime. The Qimedo is the only one that lists it.
Listings here mention bathroom and shower use, but check the page for waterproof ratings before wetting the motor.

faq.q: How do I clean the brush heads?
faq.a: Rinse them after use and let them dry. Replace worn heads.

faq.q: Can I use these on floors?
faq.a: The Leebein floor tile model is named for it, and extendable handles help with reach.

finalTake: The Qimedo Q2 is the best choice when grout is truly dirty, thanks to its stated speed and battery. The HOTO Wand suits detailed lines, and the Leebein floor tile model handles big floors. The Dovety is a low-risk starter.
